proposal: Change the arm to `&[LOG_ANALYTICS_READER, LOG_ANALYTICS_CONTRIBUTOR, READER, CONTRIBUTOR, OWNER]` and add a test mirroring `control_plane_supersets_satisfy_reader_but_not_kv_data_plane`; extend the module doc to say control-plane `*/read` satisfies Log Analytics query.

Microsoft confirms the docs are right: 'The /read permission is usually granted from a role that includes */read or * permissions, such as the built-in Reader and Contributor roles' and 'The standard Reader or Contributor roles, which include the */read action, override table-level access control' (learn.microsoft.com/azure/azure-monitor/logs/manage-access); Log Analytics Reader itself is `*/read` + Microsoft.Support/*. The module's conservatism rationale (azure_roles.rs:7-12) is about Key Vault data-plane, not control-plane query, so it does not apply. title: private_file temp path is predictable and opened without O_EXCL, so a symlink pre-planted in a shared export directory is followed — cheap hardening with create_new
rationale: The temp name is `<target>.tmp<pid>` — pid is readable by any local user — and the open is `create(true)` without `create_new`/`O_NOFOLLOW`, deliberately reusing a pre-existing temp. In a shared or world-writable export directory (the operator picks the path via a save dialog; `/tmp` or a shared drive is plausible) another local user can pre-plant `<name>.tmp<pid>` as a symlink to a file the victim owns. The write then truncates and overwrites that victim-owned file with the secret payload (fchmod on the fd succeeds because the victim owns the target), and `rename(temp, path)` moves the symlink itself into place. Result: destruction of an arbitrary victim-owned file and the secret landing where the attacker chose. The app-config directory is per-user so `settings.json` is not exposed, but the export choke point is.
proposal: Open the temp with `.create_new(true)` (O_CREAT|O_EXCL refuses to follow an existing symlink, so no libc/`O_NOFOLLOW` is needed — libc is not a direct dependency of core) and add an in-process `AtomicU64` counter to the temp name so a stale temp from a crashed run yields `AlreadyExists` once and is retried with the next suffix (or removed first). With `create_new`, the `set_permissions` call becomes belt-and-braces and its 'reused temp' comment at 73-74 should be rewritten. Add a unix-only test that a pre-existing `<name>.tmp<pid>` symlink to a decoy file causes the write to fail (or use a fresh name) and leaves the decoy untouched.
verifier_notes: The mechanics are correct: `temp_sibling` (crates/azapptoolkit-core/src/private_file.rs:57-61) yields `<target>.tmp<pid>`, and `write_then_rename` (67-75) opens with `create(true).truncate(true)` and no `create_new`/`O_NOFOLLOW`, deliberately reusing a pre-existing temp (comment at 73-74); `set_permissions` is fchmod on the followed target, so a pre-planted symlink in the destination directory is followed, truncated, overwritten with the payload, and `rename(temp, path)` (85) moves the symlink into place. export.rs:103 (every operator-chosen export, .pfx via credentials.rs:200) is the exposed call site; `settings.json` lives in the per-user config dir and is not. No test covers a symlink temp. However the severity is overstated: it needs a unix host, a world-writable/shared directory the operator picks in a save dialog, the victim's pid, and a filename that carries a to-the-second timestamp (export.rs:56-59, 153; credentials.rs:195-199), which the attacker must pre-plant before the open; Windows — the primary target per README — needs symlink privilege. Disclosure additionally requires the attacker to hold a pre-opened fd on the victim file, since the fchmod leaves it 0600. A real but narrow hardening item; the fix is cheap and standard.

title: Graph/ARM/Key Vault error bodies flow raw and uncapped into errors, logs and the UI, unlike the Exchange client's sanitized bodies
rationale: docs/DEVELOPMENT.md 'Token & secret security model' says response bodies are 'control-char-stripped and length-capped ... never a raw body that could carry token material', but only the Exchange client does this. The Graph, ARM and Key Vault clients put the full body into `Forbidden/NotFound/Api/Server`, which `?err` logs write to disk verbatim (audit.rs:1497, consent.rs:187/200, keyvault_rbac.rs:120/192, managed_identity.rs:238, keyvault.rs) and `UiError::from` shows in toasts. A proxy/WAF block page (the case post_token explicitly guards against) or a multi-MB HTML error lands unbounded in the 14-day log.
proposal: Move `sanitize_error_body` into `azapptoolkit-core` (next to `http_retry`/`http_error`) and call it at the four body-capture sites (graph transport.rs:597, arm/transport.rs, keyvault client.rs `let body_text = resp.text()...`, exchange keeps its own call). Add a shared unit test and update DEVELOPMENT.md to name the core helper.
verifier_notes: Verified: graph transport.rs:597-618 captures the raw body into Forbidden/NotFound/Api; arm/transport.rs:77-113 and keyvault/client.rs:213-244 do the same; only exchange transport.rs:293-324 sanitizes. The shared `http_error_enum!` Display (core/http_error.rs:70-81) interpolates the body, so `UiError::from` (dto/lib.rs:140-153, `err.to_string()`) shows it in toasts and `?err` logs (e.g. audit.rs:1497) write it to the rolling file verbatim. Nuance: DEVELOPMENT.md:348-351 and .claude/rules/auth.md:23 explicitly scope the sanitization claim to Exchange bodies, so this is a consistency gap in the 'never a raw body' rule rather than a doc contradiction; graph_err.rs:64-79 rewrites 403 bodies only on the scoped-feature paths. Moving the helper to core matches the 'one definition per policy' convention. Low severity is honest.

title: Key Vault `retry_class_for` doc comment contradicts itself about `setSecret` (a PUT) — clarify the deliberate same-value replay rather than reclassify PUT
rationale: `setSecret` is the PUT this function routes to `Idempotent`, yet the doc comment cites `setSecret` as the example of a write that must not be replayed. Key Vault's SET operation always appends a version, so a 502/connection reset after the service committed is replayed up to `MAX_RETRIES` times and leaves duplicate versions of the rotated client secret in the vault (and, on final failure, `rotate_app_credential` removes the app secret while a vault version already holds it). Same class of defect the core `RetryClass` doc records for `addPassword`. The repo invariant in `tests/repo_invariants/trust.rs:167` only requires the file to contain `retry_class_for(`, so a Key Vault-specific mapping is compliant.
proposal: Rewrite the doc comment at crates/azapptoolkit-keyvault/src/client.rs:261-266 to state the actual trade-off: Key Vault `PUT /secrets/{name}` appends a version on every call, so a replay after an unknown outcome can produce a second version — but the replay carries the identical value, so the current version is always correct and the only cost is a duplicate same-value version. Optionally add a wiremock test (502 then 200) asserting both PUT bodies are byte-identical and the call succeeds. Do NOT route PUT to `NonIdempotent` for this crate: that would fail the rotation on a pre-commit transient 502 and, on a post-commit one, `rotate_app_credential` (commands/keyvault.rs:123-128) would remove the freshly minted app secret while the vault already holds it — a dead value in the vault is worse than a duplicate live one.
verifier_notes: Evidence is real: client.rs:263-266 names `setSecret` as the POST/PATCH hazard example while line 269 routes PUT (which `set_secret` at client.rs:102-106 uses) to `Idempotent`; Key Vault SET does always create a new version; repo_invariants/trust.rs:150-190 only requires a `retry_class_for(` helper so a per-crate rule would be compliant. But the impact is overstated: unlike `addPassword` (core http_retry.rs:120-130, where each replay mints a DIFFERENT secret the operator never sees), the KV replay re-sends the same plaintext, so the duplicate version holds the correct value and no credential is orphaned. The proposed fix makes the rotation flow strictly more fragile (analysis above), so only the documentation half survives. Severity low.

title: `SecretValue` derives `Serialize` although nothing serialises it, so the redacted `Debug` can be bypassed by any future `serde_json::to_string`/JSON tracing field
evidence:
crates/azapptoolkit-keyvault/src/models.rs:40-43
/// `GET /secrets/{name}` — full value included.
#[derive(Clone, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct SecretValue {
    pub value: String,

models.rs:53-54 "/// Manual impl so a stray `{:?}` can't log the secret value"

`grep -rn SecretValue apps crates` outside the crate: only `KvSecretValueDto` (the IPC DTO) is used; no call serialises `SecretValue`.
rationale: The workspace treats a derived `Debug` on a secret-bearing type as a defect and hand-writes redaction, but a derived `Serialize` gives an equally direct plaintext path (`tracing` JSON layers, `serde_json::to_string` in a future export/backup) that no test guards. Since the IPC boundary uses `KvSecretValueDto`, the derive is unused surface.
proposal: Remove `Serialize` from `SecretValue` (keep `Deserialize`); if a serialiser is ever needed, implement it manually with the value redacted or gated. Consider the same for `KvSecretValueDto` if the IPC path can move to a redacted transport in future.
verifier_notes: Verified: crates/azapptoolkit-keyvault/src/models.rs:41-51 derives `Serialize` on `SecretValue`; grep for `SecretValue` outside the crate finds only comments, and inside the crate it is only deserialized (client.rs:99, :105) and mapped field-by-field into `KvSecretValueDto` (commands/keyvault.rs:60-68). The hand-written redacting `Debug` (models.rs:53-67) shows the workspace treats accidental plaintext emission as a defect; a derived `Serialize` is an equally direct path (`serde_json::to_string`, a JSON tracing layer) with no test guarding it, and removing it costs nothing. Note the workspace has no rule against `Serialize` on secret-bearing types per se (`KvSecretValueDto`, `PasswordCredential` need it for IPC), so this is a small hardening rather than a convention violation. Low.

title: `verify-full` has no Windows story, and the docs that advertise it as 'full CI parity' do not say so
evidence:
justfile:141-147
  # Unix/CI only (bash shebang, like `setup`): this is a size gate on the Linux CI
  # runner, not something a Windows dev box needs to reproduce.
  ...
  [working-directory('apps/desktop/web-rs')]
  web-itest-size:
      #!/usr/bin/env bash

justfile:329: `verify-full: _verify-core audit web-audit deny web-deny web-itest web-itest-size`

justfile:124-127 (the Windows variant of the *other* browser recipe)
  [windows]
  web-itest-auto:
      @echo "  !! SKIPPED: web-itest — Windows runs this gate in CI only."

rationale: The comment says the recipe is Unix-only "like `setup`", but `setup` has a `[windows]` twin and `web-itest-size` does not. `verify-full` — advertised in AGENTS.md, DEVELOPMENT.md and the release skill as "full CI parity" — therefore fails on a Windows box either at `web-itest` (which the Windows `web-itest-auto` variant says is CI-only there) or at `web-itest-size` ("could not find bash" unless Git Bash is on PATH). proposal: Either (a) mark `web-itest-size` `[unix]` and add a `[windows]` twin with the same LOUD-skip text `web-itest-auto` uses (justfile:124-129), plus a `[windows] verify-full` that depends on `web-itest-auto` instead of `web-itest`/`web-itest-size` — keeping the `[unix]` `verify-full:` header first so `verify_full_runs_every_gate_ci_runs` (release.rs:382 takes the first `verify-full:` line) still reads the full list; or (b) state in AGENTS.md:20/89/173, docs/DEVELOPMENT.md:90 and .claude/skills/release/SKILL.md:57 that the browser + shard-size gates are Unix/CI only and Windows contributors rely on CI for them.
verifier_notes: Evidence real: justfile:146 `web-itest-size` is a bash-shebang recipe with no `[unix]`/`[windows]` split; verify-full (justfile:329) depends on `web-itest` (not `-auto`) and `web-itest-size`; the comment at :141-142 says 'like `setup`' but setup has a `[windows]` twin (:435-437). However this is a documented, deliberate decision inside the justfile (:141-142 'Unix/CI only', :122-123 'On Windows the GUI tests stay a CI/Unix gate (matching web-itest-size)'), and docs/DEVELOPMENT.md:324-326 already says the browser gates + shard ceiling run 'on Linux' in CI — so 'bug' overstates it. The real gap is that AGENTS.md and DEVELOPMENT.md:90 advertise verify-full as CI parity with no OS caveat. Severity low.
